bib.title: Functional Benchmarks for Robust Evaluation of Reasoning Performance, and the Reasoning Gap

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Functional Benchmarks for Robust Evaluation of Reasoning Performance, and the Reasoning Gap". Saurabh Srivastava, Annarose M B, Anto P V, Shashank Menon, Ajay Sukumar, Adwaith Samod T, Alan Philipose, Stevin Prince, Sooraj Thomas (Consequent AI). Preprint; the only venue marking on the PDF is "arXiv:2402.19450v1 [cs.AI] 29 Feb 2024" (p1). 2024.

COVERAGE: 37 of 37 pages, 85,665 of 85,665 chars. Body p1-20, references p20-29 (skimmed for origins), Appendix 11 (p29-36) and Appendix 12 (p36-37) read. The appendices hold problem lists and per-category counts, no further results tables. Figures 5-10 are charts; only their axis labels and some bar values extract as text.

CLAIMS

- claim: Every model tested loses most of its static accuracy when the same problems are re-instantiated with new inputs.
  number: reasoning gap 58.35% to 80.31%
  setup: MATH test set; 13 models (GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Claude 2.1, Mistral medium, Mixtral 8x7B and Instruct, LLaMA 2 70B, WizardCoder Python 34B, Yi 34B and Chat, StripedHyena Nous and Hessian 7B, Qwen 7B); simple few-shot prompt, no CoT, pass@1; three snapshots (Oct, Nov, Dec 2023)
  quote: "Evaluated over the Q1'24 snapshot (consisting of Oct-2023, Nov-2023, Dec-2023), we find that the models have a reasoning gap varying between 58.35% and 80.31%"
  where: p9

- claim: The gap is a relative percent decrease, not percentage points, and functional accuracy is conjunctive: a problem counts only if the static version and all k snapshots are answered correctly.
  number: none
  setup: definition
  quote: "We define the functional accuracy as the accuracy of solving a test in all k snapshots and the static variant." and "The reasoning gap is the percent decrease in the accuracy between the static and functional variants."
  where: p6

- claim: GPT-4 has the smallest gap; its accuracy falls from 25.98% to 10.82%.
  number: 1299/5000 static; 541/5000 functional; gap 58.35%
  setup: as above, 3 snapshots
  quote: "GPT4 solves 1299 static QA problems (accuracy = 25.98%), and its functional accuracy with 3-snapshots is 10.82% (541/5000), giving it the lowest reasoning gap of 58.35% amongst the models tested."
  where: p14

- claim: Nearly half of GPT-4's functional accuracy comes from problems that could not be varied at all.
  number: 239 static-only (4.78%); 302 genuinely varied (6.04%)
  setup: GPT-4, same run
  quote: "239 were ungeneralizable, and their functional versions are static. This means that 4.78% of its functional accuracy can be attributed to being static." / "302 had their functional snapshots solved, giving it a 6.04% accuracy on problems that indeed were different across snapshots."
  where: p14

- claim: Only part of MATH was functionalized, chosen as the problems the tested models already solve statically.
  number: 41.2% (2060/5000)
  setup: manual rewrite into problem / solution / inputs functions
  quote: "We have functionalized 41.2% (2060/5000) of the MATH benchmark. This subset was chosen based on the portion of the benchmark that is solvable by a group of SOTA closed and OSS models, without prompting optimizations (e.g., CoT) and with pass@1."
  where: p7

- claim: Open-weight models fall further, and what survives is trivial.
  number: static 1.86%-12.28%, functional 0.52%-4.34%; 19 problems
  setup: OSS models, 3 snapshots
  quote: "The accuracy of OSS models varies between 1.86%-12.28% and it drops to 0.52%-4.34% for the functional snapshots. Only 19 problems are consistently solved across snapshots by the majority (≥ 5/10) of models."
  where: p16

- claim: Three snapshots are enough for the gap to settle.
  number: none in text (chart only)
  setup: subsets of the same three snapshots, means over 1- and 2-snapshot subsets
  quote: "We find that three snapshots suffice to stabilize the reasoning gap."
  where: p9; Figure 6 p12

- claim: The gap grows with difficulty level and is lowest on the easier subjects.
  number: none in text (Figures 7, 8)
  quote: "We find that the reasoning gap expectedly increases with difficulty levels"
  where: p12

- claim: N-gram overlap checks miss leakage routes: paraphrase, untracked provenance of starting weights, synthetic data from contaminated models, preference tuning.
  number: none
  quote: "Contamination-testing by checking for k-contiguous token sequences fails to account for various other forms in which leakage might occur"
  where: p2

- claim: Snapshots are seeded by month, and the generator code is withheld.
  number: three snapshots per quarter
  quote: "we use a hash of the month string, e.g., "Dec-2023", combined with a hash of the original text QA, as the seed." (p6); "The specific functionalization code will never be publicly accessible. Instead three snapshots will be released every quarter." (p3)

LIMITS

Conceded by the authors (Section 6, p17-18):
- Prompting was few-shot only: "the gaps are likely to be smaller with more sophisticated prompting strategies" (p1). CoT and tool use are untested.
- Claude 2.1 and Mistral models default to chain-of-thought output, "which does not work very well with the evaluation harness", so some of their gap is formatting.
- Output matching is strict; answers a human would accept are marked wrong.
- Random generators occasionally produce 10+ digit numbers that are unreasonable to compute.
- Tool use and system prompts inside closed APIs are unknown.
- Some functionalizations are shallow enough to pattern-match.

Not shown (my reading, not stated by the authors):
- The variants change inputs, not wording. This is evidence for parameterized templates, not for a paraphrase test.
- The drop is not isolated to memorization. Snapshots can be harder than the original (the examples generate words of length 6-16 and digit counts up to 10), and a conjunctive metric over four attempts falls for any noisy solver. There is no human baseline and no control for either effect.
- No per-snapshot variance or confidence intervals; the "stabilizes at 3" claim rests on subsets of the same three snapshots.
- MATH only; GSM8K, HumanEval and MBPP are future work.
- The 2,060 problems were selected because these models solved them statically.
- Dated: 2023 models, and static accuracy is low by later standards (GPT-4 at 25.98% without CoT).

BUILDS ON: MATH (Hendrycks et al., 2021) as the base benchmark. Related alternatives it names: counterfactual tasks (Wu et al., 2023, "Reasoning or reciting?"), ROSCOE (Golovneva et al., 2023), uncertainty quantification (Ye et al., 2024), task contamination (Li and Flanigan, 2023), training data extraction (Nasr et al., 2023).

CODE: Figure 2, p8, is a complete worked example (`problem(word)`, `solution(word)`, `inputs(rngs, seed)`) for the SIXTEEN probability problem. Core lines:
```
def inputs(rngs, seed):
    rngs.set_seed(seed)
    length = rngs.int_between(6, 16)
    index = rngs.int_between(0, length - 3)
```
The extraction contains a syntax error in `solution` ("common_factor = math.gcd(numerator, denominator):" with a trailing colon), and indentation is lost.

FIGURES: Figure 5, p11. "(a) Reasoning gap (note: x-axis starts at 50%), (b) Coverage: fraction of static QA that the model solves correctly that are tested functionally, (c) Static and functional accuracies." Panel (c) shows static against functional accuracy for all 13 models at once, which makes the drop immediate. Caveat: the panel (a) axis is truncated at 50%.

PROBLEMS:
- No embedded instructions found.
- Figure 5 bar values extract detached from their model labels. The label list starts with GPT-4 and the value list starts with 80.31%, but the text says GPT-4 is 58.35%, so the order is reversed or scrambled. Only GPT-4's gap can be attributed to a named model; do not cite other per-model gaps from this extraction.
- Internal inconsistency: "majority (≥ 5/10)" on p16 and in the Figure 10 caption, against "(≥ 5/9)" in the Appendix 12 heading on p36. The introduction says 9 open-weight models.
- Figures 6-8 give no numeric values in text.
